Ogden

questions.explanation: Salt Lake City was founded in 1847 at the foot of the Wasatch Range and has been the territorial and then state capital ever since. It is also Utah's largest city and the center of the Wasatch Front, where most Utahns live.

questions.question: The Great Salt Lake is unusual among large lakes because it:
questions.correctAnswer: Has no outlet to the ocean, so minerals wash in and stay, making its water much saltier than the sea in many places
distractors: Is the deepest lake in North America
Freezes solid every winter
Is filled entirely by one river
questions.explanation: Rivers carry small amounts of dissolved minerals into the Great Salt Lake and then the water escapes only by evaporation, leaving the salts behind. The lake is the largest saltwater lake in the Western Hemisphere, and only a few salt-loving organisms - like brine shrimp - thrive in most of it.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: No way out for the salt - that is why the Great Salt Lake earned its name!

questions.question: The Great Salt Lake, Utah Lake and Sevier Lake are all shrinking leftovers of a huge prehistoric lake called:
questions.correctAnswer: Lake Bonneville
distractors: Lake Deseret
Lake Uinta
Lake Sevier the Great
questions.explanation: During the last Ice Age, Lake Bonneville covered much of western Utah, almost as large as Lake Michigan is today. When its natural dam at Red Rock Pass gave way about 14,500 years ago, a catastrophic flood drained much of it northward, and the drying climate shrank the rest into today's salt lakes and salt flats.

questions.question: Long before European contact, the Ancestral Pueblo people of southeastern Utah built homes in protected alcoves high in canyon walls. These cliff dwellings, found today in places like Bears Ears and Hovenweep, were built mainly to:

questions.explanation: Ancestral Pueblo families farmed corn, beans and squash on the mesas and canyon floors and built storerooms and homes into south-facing alcoves, which stayed warmer in winter and cooler in summer. questions.question: The Fremont people, who lived across much of present-day Utah from about 300 to 1300 CE, are best known to archaeologists for combining farming with:
questions.correctAnswer: Distinctive gray pottery, clay figurines and rock imagery showing figures with elaborate headdresses

questions.question: In Utah Studies, calling Utah's tribal nations "sovereign" means that each nation:
questions.correctAnswer: Is a self-governing political community with its own government, whose relationship with the United States runs government-to-government and predates the state of Utah

Is a private cultural organization with no government powers
Was given its government by the Utah Constitution in 1896
questions.explanation: Tribal sovereignty is inherent - Native nations governed themselves for centuries before the United States existed. They arrived in Utah faster than any wagon train

questions.question: The Utah War of 1857-1858 began when President James Buchanan, believing reports of a Mormon rebellion, sent about 2,500 U.S. troops to install a new governor by force. The episode is best described as:

A conflict in which the army destroyed the pioneer settlements
A war between Utah and California over the Sierra passes
questions.explanation: Dubbed "Buchanan's Blunder" by critics, the war saw Mormon raiders burn army supply trains and Fort Bridger, forcing the troops to winter in Wyoming, while tens of thousands of Saints moved south from their homes. Mediator Thomas Kane and incoming governor Alfred Cumming settled it in 1858 - Cumming entered Salt Lake City peacefully, and Buchanan pardoned the Saints.

questions.question: On September 11, 1857, in a mountain valley in southwestern Utah, members of a Mormon militia, with some Southern Paiute participants, attacked a wagon train of Arkansas emigrants heading for California and killed about 120 men, women and older children, sparing only young children. This event, the Mountain Meadows Massacre, is taught in Utah Studies because:
questions.correctAnswer: It was the deadliest atrocity of the Utah War crisis, and Utahns - including the church itself - have had to reckon honestly with how fear, war hysteria and local decisions produced it
distractors: It was a battle between two armies of equal size
It was carried out entirely by federal troops
It never actually happened and is only a legend
questions.explanation: The Baker-Fancher party was attacked during the panic of the Utah War, after militia leaders in Cedar City chose a plan that ended in mass murder; senior church leaders in Salt Lake City learned of it too late to stop it, and only one man, John D. Lee, was ever executed for it, twenty years later. Descendants of the victims, church representatives and local community members now cooperate in caring for the memorial sites - a modern model of shared, truthful remembrance.

An attack carried out by Mormon settlers without the army
The last battle of the American Revolution

questions.question: The Black Hawk War (about 1865-1872), Utah's longest conflict between settlers and Native peoples, was fought mainly against Ute bands led in its early years by Antonga (Black Hawk). Its deepest causes were:
questions.correctAnswer: Settler occupation of Ute hunting and fishing grounds, livestock destroying Native food sources, disease, and the collapse of the older pattern of trade and negotiation
distractors: A dispute over the route of the transcontinental railroad
An argument between Ute bands about the capital city
Gold discovered inside Salt Lake City

questions.question: In February 1870 a Utah woman named Seraph Young cast a ballot in a Salt Lake City election. The event is a landmark in American history because:
questions.correctAnswer: Utah Territory had just granted women the vote, and Utah women were the first women in the modern United States to cast ballots under an equal suffrage law

The ballot was later declared illegal and destroyed uncounted

questions.question: Between 1862 and 1890 the federal government passed a ladder of laws against the Latter-day Saint practice of plural marriage (polygamy), ending with the Edmunds-Tucker Act, which disbanded the church as a corporation and took its property. questions.question: Utah does something with its state income tax that no other state does in quite the same way: by constitutional rule, income tax revenue is earmarked to fund:

questions.explanation: The earmark dates to a 1946 constitutional amendment and was broadened in 2020 to include programs for children and people with disabilities.
